title: Micro-Decisions
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Micro-decisions are the in-the-moment judgments at the core of responsive teaching—the thousands of split-second choices teachers make every lesson about whether to press on, redirect, reteach, or probe deeper. Research suggests teachers make approximately one consequential decision every ninety seconds, making the quality of those real-time judgments foundational to whether students learn or accumulate misconceptions. These decisions are grounded in the teacher's evolving mental model of the classroom, continuously updated through a four-part cycle of notice, interpret, respond, and check. Five recurring decision domains structure responsive teaching: Probe or Move On, Where Is the Gap, Stay the Course or Pivot, Whose Thinking Is Missing, and Did It Land—each requiring teachers to read classroom evidence accurately rather than follow a script. A central research finding is that expert teachers interpret events in relation to student learning and adjust accordingly, while novice teachers tend to stick to their prepared sequence even when evidence suggests it is not working. Crucially, micro-decision skill is developable rather than innate, and building it requires deliberate reflection rather than simply accumulating classroom hours.
points: Micro-decisions are not reactive noise but the primary mechanism through which teaching becomes responsive: teachers make roughly one consequential in-the-moment decision every ninety seconds, shaping whether students receive what they need or what was planned.

The quality of micro-decisions depends on the accuracy of the teacher's mental model—a richer model allows teachers to distinguish correct-for-the-wrong-reason from genuine understanding, surface hidden misconceptions, and adapt in ways that serve learning rather than just restore order.

Five recurring decision domains structure responsive teaching: deciding whether to probe or move on, locating the source of the learning gap, choosing to stay the course or pivot, ensuring every student's thinking becomes visible, and checking whether the teaching response actually worked.

Research comparing novice and expert teachers shows that experience alone does not guarantee good micro-decisions; without deliberate reflection, teaching can slip onto autopilot, with habits replacing responsiveness and the lesson becoming a linear sequence to complete rather than an evolving response to learners.

Equity is embedded in micro-decision quality: whose signals get noticed, whose understanding gets probed, and who receives corrective feedback quietly determines which students are supported and which are overlooked.
quotes: A micro-decision is the in-the-moment judgement at the heart of responsive teaching. It is the decision to ask one more question instead of moving on, to slow the pace rather than push through the lesson plan, or to revisit an explanation instead of assuming understanding.
their research suggests that teachers make approximately one consequential decision every ninety seconds to two minutes during any given lesson.

Every lesson contains hundreds of these moments. The quality of responsive teaching is determined not by whether teachers make micro-decisions but by how accurately they interpret what is happening in the room before deciding how to proceed.

teachers do not respond directly to classroom events; they respond to the meaning they assign to those events through their mental models. Expert teachers appeared to develop richer, more flexible mental models, enabling them to connect student responses to the wider learning goal, recognise when the evidence no longer matched the plan, and adapt their teaching accordingly.
Understanding develops gradually and often incompletely, and misunderstandings frequently emerge after learning is judged to have taken place.

Without deliberate reflection and refinement, teaching can slip onto autopilot, with habits replacing responsiveness. The lesson becomes a linear sequence to get through rather than a dynamic process continually informed by evidence of student learning.
Attention isn't distributed evenly — habits and assumptions can mean the same students' thinking gets noticed while others' stays invisible.
